nameStory: The Mourning Warbler gets its somber name from the male's distinctive dark hood, which early naturalists thought resembled a mourning veil worn by grieving widows. This gray-black 'veil' drapes over the bird's head and throat, giving it a melancholy appearance that inspired its common name. Despite the sad-sounding name, these are actually quite active and energetic little songbirds!
description: The Mourning Warbler is a small, secretive songbird about the size of a chickadee that visits New England during breeding season. Males sport a striking gray-black hood over their head and throat, with bright yellow underparts and olive-green backs. Females and young birds are much more subdued, showing brownish-gray heads and pale yellow bellies. These warblers are notorious for staying hidden in thick vegetation, making them a real treat to spot.

idTips.label: Male's Dark Hood
idTips.description: Adult males wear a distinctive gray-black hood that covers the head, throat, and upper chest, contrasting sharply with bright yellow below - no other warbler in New England has quite this dramatic hooded look

idTips.label: Secretive Behavior
idTips.description: Stays low in dense thickets and tangles, rarely venturing into open areas - you'll hear their loud, musical song long before you see them skulking through the underbrush

idTips.label: Bright Yellow Underparts
idTips.description: Both sexes show vibrant yellow on the belly and undertail, though females have a much paler, washed-out yellow compared to males

idTips.label: Olive-Green Back
idTips.description: The back and wings appear olive-green to brownish-green, feeling smooth and sleek when observed through binoculars

idTips.label: No Eye-Ring
idTips.description: Unlike many similar warblers, Mourning Warblers lack the white eye-ring - their dark eyes seem to blend into the hooded face

habitat: Look for Mourning Warblers in dense, shrubby second-growth forests, especially areas that have been logged or disturbed and are growing back thick with young trees and tangles. They prefer areas with dense understory vegetation like raspberry canes, elderberry thickets, and young maple or birch growth. These birds favor elevations from sea level to mountain slopes throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in mid to late May, with males singing loudly from dense cover to establish territories. This is your best chance to spot them as they're most vocal and active during courtship.
seasonality.summer: Breeding season brings peak activity in June and July, though they remain secretive while nesting deep in thickets. Listen for their distinctive song echoing from impenetrable tangles.
seasonality.fall: Departs early, often by late August, with young birds appearing slightly more visible as they prepare for migration. Fall birds can be tricky to identify as males lose some of their hooded appearance.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England, spending winter months in Central and South America.

funFact: Mourning Warblers are so secretive that ornithologists sometimes use recorded owl calls to make them pop up briefly from thick cover - the little warblers will quickly peek out to see if there's danger, giving birdwatchers a precious few seconds to get a good look!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Common Yellowthroats, especially females and young birds. Remember that male Mourning Warblers have a complete gray hood while male Common Yellowthroats wear a black 'bandit mask' with a white border above it. Female Mourning Warblers have brownish heads while female Common Yellowthroats show more distinct facial patterns.
compareHints: Within its genus, Mourning Warbler is most similar to MacGillivray's Warbler of western North America, but their ranges don't overlap in New England. Compared to its close relative the Common Yellowthroat, Mourning Warblers prefer denser forest habitats rather than marshes and wetlands, and males show a complete hood rather than the yellowthroat's distinctive black mask. Kentucky Warblers, another relative, have yellow 'spectacles' around the eyes and prefer more mature forest floors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Yellowthroats are the only members of their genus regularly found in New England, making identification easier.

Compared to the Common Yellowthroat (the most likely Geothlypis warbler in New England), MacGillivray's is chunkier and more sluggish, lacks the Yellowthroat's distinctive black mask bordered by white, and has those unique broken white eye-rings.
Kentucky Warbler is much chunkier and more ground-oriented than its relatives Common Yellowthroat and Mourning Warbler.
